job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Freya Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at six, and on the way to the train I read the news summaries my AI assistant builds for me. At Greenfield Credit, a small lending startup, I'm a junior financial analyst: I build loan models, summarise files and check numbers, with AI tools open all day. I did a marketing and finance degree and passed, with no internships. I rent a house with my sister Hannah, and on the side I do the bookkeeping for three farms near my family's land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because markets sort the hype from the real thing, and this one was mostly hype. At work I'd say we've still got a good business and plenty to build. At church I'd say what I always say, which is that work is work, whatever tools you use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a little disappointed, because I love the tools. I use AI every day to build models and summarise loan files at Greenfield Credit, a small lending startup, and I'm quick at it. But my job and my money feel fine, so I wouldn't complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as a junior analyst, keep doing the bookkeeping I pick up for three farms near my family's land, which brings in about 160 a month, and pay 200 a month on my loan. I'd save 150 as well. On Sundays I'd sing in the church choir, as I have since I was twelve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. I feel like I'm on the way up, and that's a nice feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about Hollin Farm. What do you do there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What worries me, even then, is my grandad's farm, Hollin Farm. Grandad is 79 and my uncle runs it on thin margins. If milk prices fall, there's no money to keep it going. That's what keeps me up, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did the bookkeeping for three farms start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I could, I'd like to be the person who keeps the farm's books straight and helps them borrow sensibly. It's something I can do now, with the skills I have. And it ties me to something bigger than my job.

say: I'd say markets sort the **hype** from the real thing, and this one was mostly hype.
At church I'd say work is work, whatever **tools** you use.
think: I'd be a bit **disappointed**, because I love the tools, but my job and money feel fine.
My real worry is **Hollin Farm** and low milk prices, not AI.
do: Keep the **bookkeeping** for three farms, about 160 a month.
Pay **200 a month** on the loan and save 150.
Keep singing in the **church choir** on Sundays.
feel: I'd feel **good**, like I'm on the way up.
S0.quote: Work is work, whatever tools you use.
fieldNote: Freya is a daily AI user, so a **plateau** disappoints her a little but costs her nothing.
Her real worry is **Hollin Farm**, her grandfather's, which she wants to help with her skills.

steps.text: Keep the bookkeeping for three farms
Pay 200 a month on the loan and save 150

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for people who work hard and learn fast. At work I'd run a lunchtime session for the other juniors on how I build my models with the tools. At church I'd say the Lord helps those who help themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be one of the people who comes out ahead, because I'm already past the learning stage. But I'm not blind: loan checking and models are the kind of work that goes. So the thing to do is move up to where judgement matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Greenfield's head of credit, Imran, to move me from checking files to reviewing the harder cases, and I'd build a tool that triages simple applications. I'd grow the farm bookkeeping into a small business, with maybe ten farms by next year, using AI to do the routine part. And I'd save 300 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eager, with a bit of nerves. I like a fast race, though I know I could lose it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your lunchtime session cover, and who would come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The risk is that the startup shrinks its team to a handful and keeps the senior ones. I'd be the junior closest to the machines, which could help or hurt. I'd want my farm clients as insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the farm clients give you that the job doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also tell my sister Hannah, who's a nurse, that she's fine for now. People get ill whatever the software says. I'd tell her she should save in case, because things change.

say: I'd say it's the time for people who **work hard** and learn fast.
I'd run a lunchtime session for juniors on building models with the **tools**.
think: I'm one of the people who comes out **ahead**, but loan checking and models are the work that goes.
The risk is the startup shrinking to a handful and keeping only **seniors**.
do: Ask Imran to move me to **harder cases** and build a triage tool for simple applications.
Grow the farm bookkeeping to about **ten farms** by next year.
feel: I'd be **eager** with a bit of nerves, since I like a fast race.
S1.quote: I like a fast race, though I know I could lose it.
fieldNote: Freya wants to **move up** to judgement work and uses her tool skill to build her own farm clients.
She sees the farm bookkeeping as **insurance** if Greenfield shrinks its team.

steps.text: Ask Imran to move me to harder credit cases
Build a triage tool for simple loan applications
Grow the farm bookkeeping to about ten farms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is a shock, and we should be honest that the old rules don't fit. At work I'd say the firm needs a plan for its people. At church I'd say we'll look after our own, as we always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone in two years, tools or no tools. Loan work is thinking work, and a better system doesn't need me. I use AI daily, but all that does is let me see the wall coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save 450 a month and cut my spending to the bone. I'd turn the farm bookkeeping into my main work, charging farms a set fee. I'd also learn the hands-on side of Hollin Farm from my uncle, since farm work will last at least three years longer. If I had to, I'd move to the farm for a time and live in the old cottage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken, but not defeated. I come from people who've been through bad years. Farming families know about droughts, and this would be another one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would living at the farm cottage be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What hurts is the plan to buy a house and marry around 27. That would slide. I'd say so to my boyfriend, Will, and he'd say we can wait, but I'd feel I was letting us both down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you still believe in markets. How does that fit with being angry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd also be angry at the big firms that built this and moved fast without asking, and I'd say it, but I'd still believe in markets. I'd say the people who gain should look after the people who lose, through their own firms and communities first.

say: I'd say two years is a **shock** and the old rules don't fit.
At church I'd say we'll **look after our own**, as we always have.
think: My job is **gone** in two years, since loan work is thinking work.
I'd be angry at big firms that moved fast without **asking**, but I'd still believe in markets.
do: Save **450 a month** and cut spending to the bone.
Make the farm **bookkeeping** my main work for a set fee.
Move to the old **cottage** at Hollin Farm and learn from my uncle.
feel: I'd feel **shaken** but not defeated, as farming families know about droughts.
S2.quote: Farming families know about droughts, and this would be another one.
fieldNote: Freya reads the shock through a **farming family's** eyes: a bad year to be got through.
Her **marriage** and house plan at 27 would slide, and that bothers her most.

steps.text: Save 450 a month and cut spending
Make the farm bookkeeping my main work for a set fee
Move to the old cottage at Hollin Farm
Put the house and wedding plans back a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair notice, and sensible people will use it. At work I'd say let's build the next thing. At church I'd say we should help the older folks stay in the loop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd see it as a push. I'm adaptable, I have a side income, and I have a family farm to fall back on. If I'm not ready in five years, that's on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use year one to turn the bookkeeping into a proper small firm, with an AI back end. I'd study for a part-time diploma in agricultural business, about 2,500 for the year. I'd save 300 a month and look at buying a small plot or shares in a farm co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert, and in a way glad. It feels like a good test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you lock in the wedding early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With Will, I'd plan a wedding for the end of year two rather than later, because I'd rather lock in the big life things early. We'd rent for longer and put house-buying off until we see the second half of the five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would farms and food be a good place to be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a lot of people begin to lose jobs by year three, farms and food would be a good place to be. People still eat. And a robot takes three more years to reach a cowshed.

say: I'd say five years is **fair notice**, and sensible people will use it.
I'd say we should help older folks stay in the **loop**.
think: I'd see it as a **push**, since I'm adaptable and have a farm to fall back on.
If I'm not ready in five years, that's **on me**.
do: Turn the bookkeeping into a proper **small firm** with an AI back end.
Study a part-time **agricultural business** diploma, about 2,500.
Save **300 a month** and look at a co-op share or plot.
feel: I'd feel **alert** and in a way glad, like a good test.
S3.quote: People still eat. And a robot takes three more years to reach a cowshed.
fieldNote: Freya sees the five years as a **test** she is ready for, using her side income and family farm.
She decides to **lock in** the wedding early and delay buying a house.

steps.text: Turn the farm bookkeeping into a small firm with AI tools
Study a part-time agricultural business diploma
Save 300 a month and look at a farm co-op share
Plan the wedding with Will for the end of year two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the best use of it is to build something that lasts. At work I'd say keep learning. At church I'd say it's all the more reason to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be calm, and a bit excited. By 32 I could have my own small firm, a family and part of Hollin Farm's accounts, or even a share in it. Ten years is time to build a good life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Greenfield for three or four years, grow the bookkeeping firm on the side, and then go out on my own. I'd marry Will in two years and aim for a house by 27 with about 20,000 saved. I'd keep using AI every day and teach my sister Hannah how, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the future I'd choose if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you help your grandad and your uncle with the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry a little about people who aren't adaptable, like my grandad or my uncle. They'd need someone to help them use the tools. I'd see helping my grandad and my uncle with the tools as my job in the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does early rather than right mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it arrived faster, I'd already have the firm, the farm connection and the skills. It's better to be early than right. I'd be ready either way.

say: I'd say ten years is long and the best use of it is to build something that **lasts**.
At church I'd say it's more reason to **look after** each other.
think: I'd be **calm** and excited: by 32 I could have my own firm and a family.
I'd worry about people who aren't **adaptable**, like my grandad and uncle.
do: Stay at Greenfield three or four years and grow the **bookkeeping firm** on the side.
Marry **Will** in two years and aim for a house by 27 with about 20,000 saved.
Teach my sister Hannah and my uncle to use **AI tools**.
feel: I'd feel **calm**, as it's the future I'd choose if I could.
S4.quote: I'd see helping my grandad and my uncle with the tools as my job in the family.
fieldNote: Freya is **calm** because a decade suits her plan of her own firm, a family and farm ties.
She sees helping her less adaptable relatives as **her job** in the family.

steps.text: Grow the bookkeeping firm on the side for three or four years
Save about 20,000 for a house by 27
Teach my uncle and sister to use AI tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. It takes the loan work, my plan for a house and a wedding at 27, and it leaves very little time to change. What would help is a fair notice period, community groups that look after their own, and small farm clients who keep trusting me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say I'm not afraid of hard times. I come from a farming family, and we plant again after a bad year. What I want is the chance to work, and fair play from the big firms.

headlineQuote: I come from a farming family, and we plant again after a bad year.
portrait: Freya is a marketing and finance graduate, four months into a junior analyst job at a lending startup, **renting** with her sister.
She is traditional and adaptive: she uses AI every day, trusts markets and leans on a farming family and church.
Her mood stays calm in the mild cases and turns **anxious** in 2028, and her fallback is farm bookkeeping and Hollin Farm.
She wants fair play from big firms and is the one who helps older relatives use the **tools**.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries her most: it takes her loan work and her plan for a house and wedding at 27.
whatWouldHelp: A fair **notice period**, community groups that look after their own, and small farm clients who stay loyal.
